content: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) refers to any preventive medical treatment initiated immediately after exposure to a disease-causing agent, such as a virus, with the goal of preventing the onset of the disease. PEP is widely used and highly effective in preventing rabies following a bite from a rabid animal. The standard treatment for rabies involves a series of repeated injections of the rabies vaccine along with immunoglobulin. In the context of HIV exposure, PEP is recommended after high-risk events such as unprotected anal or vaginal intercourse, needlestick injuries, or sharing needles. For PEP to be effective, it must be started as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within one hour. The treatment regimen for HIV-related PEP lasts for four weeks. While there is strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of PEP in preventing HIV infection, there have been documented cases where it has failed. The treatment regimen for PEP can be challenging to adhere to and is often associated with unpleasant side effects. These side effects may include general malaise, fatigue, diarrhea, headaches, nausea, and vomiting. According to an Australian study, approximately two-thirds of individuals taking PEP reported experiencing mild to moderate side effects, while one-quarter of individuals experienced severe side effects.
